summary.text: A review of Unit 4 lessons 4-1 to 4-4: multiplying decimals by powers of 10, estimating products, and multiplying a decimal by a whole number, with a third of it on finding the mistake in a worked answer.

why.text: The test checks whether she can multiply, and also whether she catches her own slips. This review practises both.

objectives.text: Multiply a decimal by a power of 10
Estimate a product and say whether it is over or under
Multiply a decimal by a whole number and place the point
Find the slip in a worked answer and say which check catches it

parentNote.text: Built from the lesson 4-1 to 4-4 practice pages in her Unit 4 folder and the 11/13 newsletter, with fresh numbers that neither the pages nor the four lessons use. This is Part 1: the newsletter says lessons 4-5 to 4-8 are taught the week of 11/16, and their pages are not in Drive yet, so they are not covered here. Part 2 can be built when they arrive. No test date is printed yet. Seven questions give a wrong worked answer and ask which slip made it; two ask which check catches a slip, including one an estimate misses (2 × 0.47 written as 0.814), which is why counting decimal places matters too.

nextUp.text: Work each one out yourself before you look at the choices, then check it two ways.

cards.def:
**Multiplying by 10, 100 or 10³ moves the point right, one place for each zero.**
• 3.08 × 10² = 308.
• The exponent counts the zeros; it is never a factor.

**Round to friendly numbers and multiply in your head.**
• 7.92 × 31 → 8 × 30 = 240.
• For a decimal less than 1, use 0.5 or 0.25, never 0.
**Round both factors up and you overestimate; round both down and you underestimate.**

**Multiply as whole numbers, then give the product as many decimal places as the factors have.**
• 0.86 × 9 → 86 × 9 = 774 → 7.74.

**Round and multiply: an answer about ten times too big or small means the point slipped.**
• 0.58 × 9 is about 5.4, so 52.2 is wrong.

**The product has as many decimal places as the factors (before you drop end zeros).**
• 2 × 0.47 cannot be 0.814: three places where there should be two.

**Times a power of 10 grows; times a decimal less than 1 shrinks.**
• 0.64 × 8 must be less than 8, so 512 is wrong.
cards.hint: Ask which way the answer should go.

cards.def: **Watch for the point moving the wrong way, one place too few or too many, or 10³ read as 30.**

**Watch for the point left out or misplaced, no regrouping, a dropped zero, or adding instead of multiplying.**
• 3 × 1.27 is 3.81, not 3.621.
• 4.15 × 60 is 249, not 24.9.
cards.hint: Name the slip, then fix it.

cards.def: **Work it out yourself, compare with the wrong answer, then ask what move would make that number.**
cards.hint: Every wrong answer came from somewhere.

questions.q: Jada worked out 4.06 × 10³ and wrote 0.00406. What went wrong?
opts: The point moved left, the wrong way
The point moved one place too few
The point moved one place too many
The exponent was used as a factor
questions.hint: Should the answer be bigger or smaller than 4.06?
steps: 10³ = 1,000, so the point should move 3 places to the right.
The right answer is 4,060.
0.00406 is what you get when the point moved left, the wrong way.
Check: multiplying by 1,000 makes a number bigger, and 0.00406 did not grow.

ex.main: **The point moved left, the wrong way.** The right answer is 4,060.
ex.tip: Multiplying by a power of 10 always makes a number bigger.

questions.q: Owen worked out 0.73 × 10² and wrote 7.3. What went wrong?
opts: The point moved left, the wrong way
The point moved one place too few
The point moved one place too many
The exponent was used as a factor
steps: 10² = 100, so the point should move 2 places to the right.
The right answer is 73.
7.3 is what you get when the point moved one place too few.
Check: multiplying by 100 makes a number bigger, and 7.3 grew by the wrong amount.

ex.main: **The point moved one place too few.** The right answer is 73.
ex.tip: Count the zeros, then count your moves.

questions.q: Nia worked out 2.9 × 10³ and wrote 87. What went wrong?
opts: The point moved one place too few
The point moved left, the wrong way
The exponent was used as a factor
The point moved one place too many
questions.hint: What does 10³ mean? It is not 10 × 3.
steps: 10³ = 1,000, so the point should move 3 places to the right.
The right answer is 2,900.
87 is what you get when the exponent was used as a factor.
Check: multiplying by 1,000 makes a number bigger, and 87 grew by the wrong amount.

ex.main: **The exponent was used as a factor.** The right answer is 2,900.
ex.tip: The exponent counts tens; it is never a factor.

questions.q: Eli worked out 0.64 × 8 and wrote 512. What went wrong?
opts: The numbers were added, not multiplied
The point went one place too far right
The point went one place too far left
The decimal point was left out
steps: Multiply as whole numbers: 8 × 64 = 512.
0.64 has 2 decimal places, so the product is 5.12.
512 is what you get when the decimal point was left out.
Check with an estimate: 0.6 × 8 is about 4.8.

ex.main: **The decimal point was left out.** The right answer is 5.12.
ex.tip: Times a number less than 1 makes the answer smaller than 8.

questions.q: Rosa worked out 3 × 1.27 and wrote 3.621. What went wrong?
opts: Each place was multiplied, not regrouped
The decimal point was left out
The point went one place too far right
The numbers were added, not multiplied
steps: Multiply as whole numbers: 3 × 127 = 381.
1.27 has 2 decimal places, so the product is 3.81.
3.621 is what you get when each place was multiplied, not regrouped.
Check with an estimate: 1 × 3 is about 3.

ex.main: **Each place was multiplied, not regrouped.** The right answer is 3.81.
ex.tip: Regroup: 21 hundredths is 2 tenths and 1 hundredth.

questions.q: Sam worked out 4.15 × 60 and wrote 24.9. What went wrong?
opts: The point went one place too far right
The zero in the whole number was dropped
The decimal point was left out
The numbers were added, not multiplied
steps: Multiply as whole numbers: 60 × 415 = 24,900.
4.15 has 2 decimal places, so the product is 249.
24.9 is what you get when the zero in the whole number was dropped.
Check with an estimate: 4 × 60 is about 240.

ex.main: **The zero in the whole number was dropped.** The right answer is 249.
ex.tip: A zero in the whole number is part of it.

questions.q: Ivy worked out 0.45 × 8 and wrote 8.45. What went wrong?
opts: The point went one place too far right
The decimal point was left out
The numbers were added, not multiplied
The point went one place too far left
steps: Multiply as whole numbers: 8 × 45 = 360.
0.45 has 2 decimal places, so the product is 3.6.
8.45 is what you get when the numbers were added, not multiplied.
Check with an estimate: 0.5 × 8 is about 4.

ex.main: **The numbers were added, not multiplied.** The right answer is 3.6.
ex.tip: Read the sign before you start.

questions.q: Ben wrote 2 × 0.47 = 0.814. That is close to his estimate, 2 × 0.5 = 1. Which check shows his answer is wrong?
opts: Whole numbers: a whole number times anything is whole
The estimate: 0.814 is far too far from 1 to be right
No check does; being close to 1 means 0.814 is right
Counting places: 0.47 has two, so the answer cannot have three
questions.hint: An estimate only says roughly how big. What else can you check?
steps: 0.814 is close to 1, so the estimate does not catch it.
0.47 has two decimal places, so the product has two. 0.814 has three.
He wrote 2 × 4 = 8 and 2 × 7 = 14 side by side instead of regrouping.

ex.main: **Counting places.** 0.47 has two decimal places, so the product has two: 0.94. 0.814 slips past the estimate because it is close to 1, which is why one check is not always enough.
ex.tip: Use more than one check. Each one catches different slips.

questions.q: Mia wrote 0.58 × 9 = 52.2. Which check shows her answer is wrong?
opts: An estimate: 0.6 × 9 = 5.4, so 52.2 is about ten times too big
Counting places: 52.2 has one place, so the point is fine
Nothing: 58 × 9 = 522, so 52.2 checks out
Rounding 9 to 10: 0.58 × 10 = 58, so 52.2 is close enough
questions.hint: Round 0.58 to a friendly decimal and multiply.
steps: 0.58 is about 0.6.
52.2 is about ten times 5.4, so the point slipped one place.
The right answer is 5.22.

ex.main: **An estimate.** 0.6 × 9 = 5.4, and 52.2 is ten times too big. The right answer is 5.22. (0.58 × 10 is 5.8, not 58.)
ex.tip: An answer about ten times too big or small means the point slipped.

questions.q: What is 3.08 × 10²?
questions.hint: Count the zeros in 100. Keep the zero inside 3.08.
steps: 10² = 100, so the point moves 2 places to the right.
One place at a time: 3.08 → 30.8 → 308.

ex.main: **308.** 100 has 2 zeros, so the point moves 2 places right.
ex.tip: A zero inside a number stays.

questions.q: What is 0.052 × 10⁴?
steps: 10⁴ = 10,000, so the point moves 4 places to the right.

ex.main: **520.** 10,000 has 4 zeros, so the point moves 4 places right.
ex.tip: Fill empty places with zeros as you move.

questions.q: What is 0.86 × 9?
steps: Multiply as whole numbers: 9 × 86 = 774.
0.86 has 2 decimal places, so the product has 2: 7.74.
Check with an estimate: about 8.1.

ex.main: **7.74.** 774 is what you get when the decimal point was left out; 77.4 is what you get when the point went one place too far right; 0.774 is what you get when the point went one place too far left.
ex.tip: Estimate: 0.9 × 9 is about 8.

questions.q: What is 12 × 4.05?
steps: Multiply as whole numbers: 12 × 405 = 4,860.
4.05 has 2 decimal places, so the product has 2: 48.60.
Check with an estimate: about 48.

ex.main: **48.6.** 4,860 is what you get when the decimal point was left out; 486 is what you get when the point went one place too far right; 4.86 is what you get when the point went one place too far left.
ex.tip: Estimate: 12 × 4 = 48.

questions.q: What is 3.15 × 20?
steps: Multiply as whole numbers: 20 × 315 = 6,300.
3.15 has 2 decimal places, so the product has 2: 63.00.
Check with an estimate: about 60.

ex.main: **63.** 6.3 is what you get when the zero in the whole number was dropped; 630 is what you get when the point went one place too far right; 6,300 is what you get when the decimal point was left out.
ex.tip: Multiply by 20, not by 2.

questions.q: What is 0.004 × 25?
steps: Multiply as whole numbers: 25 × 4 = 100.
0.004 has 3 decimal places, so the product has 3: 0.100.
Check with an estimate: about 0.

ex.main: **0.1.** 100 is what you get when the decimal point was left out; 1 is what you get when the point went one place too far right; 0.01 is what you get when the point went one place too far left.
ex.tip: Three places: write zeros after the point if you need them.

questions.q: Which is the best estimate of 7.92 × 31?
questions.hint: Round 7.92 to the nearest whole number and 31 to the nearest ten.
steps: 7.92 rounds to 8.
31 rounds to 30.

ex.main: **240.** 8 × 30 = 240. 210 chops 7.92 down to 7 instead of rounding it to 8, and 24 and 2,400 put the point in the wrong place.
ex.tip: 7.92 is almost 8. Round it, do not chop it.

questions.q: Rounding each factor to the nearest whole number, which gives an OVERestimate?
questions.hint: An overestimate needs the factors to round up.
steps: 3.6 rounds up to 4, and 4.7 rounds up to 5.
4 × 5 = 20 is more than the exact 16.92.
In each of the others, both factors round down.

ex.main: **3.6 × 4.7.** Both factors round up, so 4 × 5 = 20 is more than the exact 16.92. Every other pair rounds both factors down.
ex.tip: Both up, over. Both down, under.

questions.q: Ribbon costs $0.85 a yard. Lila buys 14 yards. How much does she pay?
steps: 0.85 has two decimal places: 11.90.
Check: $1 × 14 = $14, a little more than $11.90.

ex.main: **$11.90.** 85 × 14 = 1,190, and two places makes 11.90. $14.85 adds instead of multiplying, and the others misplace the point.
ex.tip: Money keeps two places.

questions.q: A trail is 2.75 km long. Theo walks it there and back, on 3 days. How far does he walk in all?
opts: 5.5 km
165 km
steps: There and back is 2 trips a day: 6 trips in all.
Check: about 3 km × 6 = 18 km.

ex.main: **16.5 km.** 2.75 × 6 = 16.5. 8.25 counts only the trip there, 5.5 is one day, and 165 drops the point.
ex.tip: Count every trip the story mentions.

questions.q: Which equation is NOT true?
questions.hint: Check where the point goes in each product.
steps: 48 × 0.5 has one decimal place: 24.0, which is 24.
0.48 × 5 has two: 2.40, which is 2.4.
4.8 × 5 has one place: 24.0, so it is 24, not 2.4.

ex.main: **4.8 × 5 = 2.4.** 4.8 has one decimal place, so the product is 24.0, which is 24. The other three are true.
ex.tip: Count the places in the factors; the product has the same.
